site_article.headline: Claude apps will run in auto mode by default on Pro, Max and Team plans
site_article.dek: Anthropic is bringing the permission setting it made standard in Claude Code to the Claude web, desktop and mobile apps, with an automated check in place of step-by-step approvals.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic is changing how much Claude asks before it acts. In a post on its official Claude account on October 22, 2026, the company said that starting the following week, sessions across the Claude web, desktop and mobile apps will run in auto mode by default for subscribers on the Pro, Max and Team plans.

According to the post, Claude will no longer ask users to approve each step. An automated check will block risky actions instead, and users can switch back to manual approvals at any time. The company did not give an exact start date beyond the following week.

WinCentral, which reported the change on October 23, described the system as a safety classifier that runs alongside the model. Harmless, routine and read-only actions are approved immediately, the outlet said, while risky actions such as unexpected script execution or irreversible changes to data are blocked. When an action is flagged, Claude either looks for a safer way to finish the task or asks the user for approval.

Anthropic has already used this approach in Claude Code, its coding tool. In an article published on August 7, 2026, the company said auto mode would become the default for new Claude Code sessions on the Pro, Max and Team plans starting August 14. It explained that each tool call passes through a classifier aimed at actions that are irreversible, destructive or directed outside the user's environment.

The same article described several limits on the system. If Claude is blocked three times in a row, or twenty times in one session, Claude Code falls back to manual approvals. Permission rules that users set still run before the classifier, and Anthropic said broad rules that would allow arbitrary code to run are set aside while auto mode is on.

Anthropic's case for auto mode rests on its own testing. In a controlled study described in the August article, people reviewing dangerous commands stopped 13.6 percent of them, while auto mode blocked 89 percent. The company also reported that human reviewers became less careful as sessions went on, with their block rate falling from about 17 percent early in a session to about 5 percent after more than 50 prompts, while the automated check held steady.

Anthropic was careful about how far those results reach. It said one figure on the classifier's miss rate, measured after hardening it against attacks from an outside red team, should not be read as the miss rate on real traffic. WinCentral noted that it could not review the methodology behind the comparison between people and the classifier.

For Claude Code, Anthropic said users can leave auto mode with Shift+Tab in the command line tool or through the mode menu in the desktop app, and that administrators can set a default mode or turn auto mode off in managed settings. WinCentral reported that users of the Claude apps can switch modes from the session controls and set their preferred default in their account settings.

The change reflects a problem that grows as AI assistants take on longer tasks. A prompt for every small action quickly becomes noise, and Anthropic's own data suggests people start approving requests without reading them. Moving the routine decisions to an automated reviewer is a bet that a consistent check will catch more real danger than a tired person clicking yes. It also means most paid Claude users will now rely on Anthropic's classifier by default rather than on their own judgment at each step, so the quality of that classifier matters more than before.

The next thing to watch is how the setting behaves once it reaches millions of everyday app sessions, including whether Anthropic publishes figures for the Claude apps similar to the ones it released for Claude Code.
